lessons.title: Consensus with Raft: elections, log replication and safety
lessons.summary: How Raft keeps a replicated log consistent: terms, elections, the commit rule, the safety argument, linearizable reads, membership changes, and how it compares to Paxos.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Consensus means getting several machines to agree on a sequence of decisions even when some crash, restart or get cut off. Raft agrees on a **replicated log** of commands. If every replica applies the same commands in the same order to the same deterministic state machine, every replica ends in the same state. This **replicated state machine** model is how etcd (and so Kubernetes), Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV and Kafka's KRaft controller stay consistent.

Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout (USENIX ATC 2014) designed Raft for understandability, splitting it into **leader election**, **log replication** and **safety**. This lesson follows that split.

Two numbers frame everything:
- A cluster of `2f + 1` voters tolerates `f` failures. 3 nodes tolerate 1, 5 tolerate 2.
- Every write costs at least one round trip from the leader to a majority, plus a durable disk write (fsync) on each of them. Consensus is never free.

## Roles, terms and the two RPCs
Every node is a **follower**, a **candidate** or the **leader**. Time is divided into numbered **terms**; each starts with an election and has at most one leader. Terms are a logical clock: a higher term in any message makes the receiver adopt it and step down; a stale term is rejected.

Raft needs only two RPCs:
- `RequestVote(term, candidateId, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm)`: sent by candidates.
- `AppendEntries(term, leaderId, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries[], leaderCommit)`: sent by the leader to replicate entries, and with no entries as a heartbeat.

(`InstallSnapshot` ships a snapshot to a follower that is far behind.) Each node persists `currentTerm`, `votedFor` and its log before answering; losing them could let a node vote twice in one term.

## Leader election step by step
```text
follower --(no heartbeat within election timeout)--> candidate
candidate: currentTerm++, vote for self, send RequestVote to all
   - votes from a majority          -> leader, send heartbeats immediately
   - sees AppendEntries from a leader with term >= its own -> follower
   - timeout with no winner (split vote) -> new term, try again
```

1. Followers expect heartbeats. If none arrives within the **election timeout**, the follower assumes the leader is dead.
2. It increments its term, becomes a candidate, votes for itself and asks everyone else for a vote.
3. A node grants at most one vote per term, first come first served, **and only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date as its own** (the election restriction, explained under safety).
4. A candidate with votes from a majority becomes leader and starts sending heartbeats.

Split votes are resolved by **randomised timeouts** (the paper suggests 150 to 300 ms in a LAN) so one node usually times out first and wins. etcd defaults to a 100 ms heartbeat and a 1000 ms election timeout, tuned to network round-trip time. Too short and a GC pause or slow disk triggers needless elections; too long and failover is slow.

Two additions in etcd and other implementations:
- **PreVote**: a node asks "would you vote for me?" before bumping its term, so a node returning from isolation with a huge term cannot depose a healthy leader.
- **CheckQuorum**: a leader that has not heard from a majority recently steps down.

## Log replication step by step
Clients send commands only to the leader (followers redirect or proxy).

```text
client -> leader: SET x=5
leader: append (index 7, term 3, SET x=5) to its log
leader -> followers: AppendEntries(prevLogIndex=6, prevLogTerm=3, entries=[7])
followers: check they have entry 6 with term 3; if so append 7, fsync, ack
leader: entry 7 is on a majority (itself + 2 of 4) -> commitIndex = 7
leader: apply to state machine, reply to client
next AppendEntries carries leaderCommit=7 -> followers apply up to 7
```

The `prevLogIndex` / `prevLogTerm` check is the heart of it. A follower only accepts new entries if its log matches the leader's at the entry just before them. If the check fails, the leader decrements its `nextIndex` for that follower and retries further back until they agree, then overwrites the follower's conflicting suffix. By induction this gives the **Log Matching Property**: if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, the logs are identical up to that index.

Note what the leader never does: it never deletes or overwrites its own entries (**Leader Append-Only**). Followers' uncommitted tails can be thrown away; the leader's log is the truth for its term.

## The commit rule, and the subtle part
An entry is **committed** when it is safe to apply, meaning it will survive any future leader change. The rule:

> The leader marks an entry committed once it is stored on a majority **and it was created in the leader's current term**. Committing it also commits every entry before it.

Why the second half? Figure 8 of the Raft paper shows the trap. Suppose a leader in term 2 replicates entry X to a minority and crashes. A later leader in term 4 re-replicates X to a majority by bringing followers in line. X is now on a majority, but it is still from term 2. If that leader crashes before writing anything in term 4, a node that never had X but has a term-3 entry at the same index can win an election (its last log term, 3, beats a log ending in 2) and overwrite X everywhere. So "on a majority" is not enough for old-term entries. Once the term-4 leader commits an entry from term 4 on top of X, any future leader must have that term-4 entry, and hence X.

This is why new leaders commonly append a **no-op entry** at the start of their term: committing it immediately commits everything before it and tells the leader what its commit index really is.

## Safety in one paragraph
The guarantee that matters is **Leader Completeness**: if an entry is committed in some term, it is present in the log of every leader of a later term. The argument: a committed entry is on a majority. A candidate needs votes from a majority. Two majorities overlap in at least one node. That node will refuse to vote for a candidate whose log is less up to date (compare the last entry's term first, then the index). So the winner's log contains the entry. Combined with Log Matching, every state machine applies the same command at the same index (**State Machine Safety**).

Raft does not guarantee **liveness** under arbitrary timing. The FLP result says no deterministic algorithm can guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash; Raft relies on timeouts and randomisation to make progress in practice, never trading away safety.

## Partitions, odd sizes and membership
```text
5 nodes: A B | C D E
- If the leader was A: A cannot reach a majority, CheckQuorum makes it step down,
  its uncommitted writes never commit.
- C D E elect a new leader in a higher term and keep serving.
- When the partition heals, A and B see the higher term, step down,
  and their conflicting uncommitted tails are overwritten.
```

Why odd sizes? A 4-node cluster needs 3 for a majority and still tolerates only 1 failure, like 3 nodes. Even sizes add cost, not resilience. Five survives a failure during maintenance; more than 7 voters is rare.

**Membership changes**: switching every node from C-old to C-new at once can briefly allow two disjoint majorities. The paper uses **joint consensus**; most implementations use the simpler **one server at a time** change from Ongaro's dissertation. etcd adds **learners**, non-voting members that catch up before promotion.

**Log compaction**: nodes snapshot their state machine and discard the log prefix; a follower behind the snapshot gets `InstallSnapshot`.

## Linearizable reads without writing to the log
The simplest correct read is to append the read to the log and answer when it commits. It works but costs a disk write per read. Two cheaper options:

- **ReadIndex**: the leader records its current commit index, sends a heartbeat round to confirm a majority still accepts it as leader, waits until its state machine has applied up to that index, then answers. Cost: one network round trip, no disk write. etcd uses this for its default linearizable reads.
- **Lease reads**: after a successful heartbeat round, the leader assumes nobody else can become leader for slightly less than the election timeout and serves reads locally. Fastest, but correctness now depends on bounded clock drift. A paused leader (stop-the-world GC, VM migration) can serve stale data.

Follower reads are stale unless the follower first asks the leader for the read index. etcd offers linearizable reads by default, or `serializable` reads answered locally by any member.

## Real systems
- **etcd** runs one Raft group for the whole keyspace, which is why its data size stays small and why Kubernetes cares about etcd disk latency.
- **CockroachDB** uses **Multi-Raft**: each range (default max 512 MiB) is its own Raft group, with heartbeats coalesced between nodes. Reads go to the **leaseholder**, normally colocated with the Raft leader. TiKV and YugabyteDB do the same.
- **Kafka KRaft** replaced ZooKeeper with a Raft quorum of controllers. **Spanner** and **Chubby** use Paxos; **ZooKeeper** uses Zab.

## Raft vs Paxos
Real systems use **Multi-Paxos** (a stable leader, one Paxos instance per log slot), which in steady state looks just like Raft. Howard and Mortier's "Paxos vs Raft" paper shows the differences are mostly in leader election: Raft only elects a leader whose log is already up to date, so it never has to recover entries from others, and Raft's log has **no holes**, whereas Multi-Paxos can decide slots out of order. Raft was also specified end to end (membership, snapshots), where Paxos left much to the implementer. etcd and CockroachDB chose Raft for that completeness and a well-tested library; neither is faster in principle.

## Code: the follower side of AppendEntries
A simplified Go-style version of the receiver logic, close to Figure 2 of the paper:

```go
func (n *Node) AppendEntries(a AppendArgs) AppendReply {
    n.mu.Lock()
    defer n.mu.Unlock()
    if a.Term < n.currentTerm {
        return AppendReply{Term: n.currentTerm, Success: false} // stale leader
    }
    if a.Term > n.currentTerm {
        n.currentTerm, n.votedFor = a.Term, -1
    }
    n.state = Follower
    n.resetElectionTimer()

    // consistency check: do we have the entry just before the new ones?
    if a.PrevLogIndex > n.lastIndex() || n.termAt(a.PrevLogIndex) != a.PrevLogTerm {
        return AppendReply{Term: n.currentTerm, Success: false}
    }
    // delete a conflicting suffix, then append anything new
    for i, e := range a.Entries {
        idx := a.PrevLogIndex + 1 + i
        if idx <= n.lastIndex() && n.termAt(idx) != e.Term {
            n.truncateFrom(idx)
        }
        if idx > n.lastIndex() {
            n.append(a.Entries[i:]...)
            break
        }
    }
    n.persist() // fsync term, vote and log before replying
    if a.LeaderCommit > n.commitIndex {
        n.commitIndex = min(a.LeaderCommit, n.lastIndex())
    }
    return AppendReply{Term: n.currentTerm, Success: true}
}
```

Notice `persist()` before the reply. An implementation that acks before fsync can lose a committed entry if a majority crash at once.

## Trade-offs and when not to use it
- **Latency**: every write waits for a majority; across regions that is a WAN round trip. Place voters so a majority sits close together.
- **Throughput**: one leader serialises writes for its group. Scale with many groups (one per shard), not bigger groups.
- **Not for everything**: data that merges (counters, carts, presence) is better served by leaderless replication or CRDTs. Use consensus for one agreed order: leader election, locks, configuration, balances, uniqueness.
- **Do not build your own**: use etcd, a database that embeds Raft, or a mature library.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Thinking "on a majority" means committed** for old-term entries (the Figure 8 bug).
- **Not persisting before replying**, or using a disk with a write cache that lies about fsync.
- **Election storms**: frequent leader changes in metrics usually mean the election timeout is too close to disk or GC latency. Check fsync duration (etcd exposes `etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds`) before blaming the network.
- **Stale reads from a deposed leader** when someone "optimised" reads by skipping ReadIndex.
- **Treating leadership as a lock** without fencing: a paused process can wake up after a new leader exists, so downstream systems should check the term or a fencing token.
- Jepsen's analyses (etcd, Consul and others) show how real implementations got these details wrong, such as stale reads later fixed with ReadIndex-style checks.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you understand *why* Raft is safe, not just the happy path. Expect "what if the leader crashes right after replicating to one follower?", "why majorities?", and "how do you read without going through the log?".

**60-second answer outline:**
1. Raft keeps a replicated log so every replica applies the same commands in order.
2. One leader per term, elected by majority with randomised timeouts; voters only vote for candidates whose log is at least as up to date.
3. The leader appends, replicates with AppendEntries and a prev-index/term check, and commits once a majority has the entry from its current term.
4. Majority overlap plus the vote restriction means every future leader has all committed entries.
5. Linearizable reads need ReadIndex or a lease; membership changes go one server at a time or via joint consensus.

**Follow-ups to expect:** Figure 8 and the no-op entry; PreVote and CheckQuorum; why 4 nodes is pointless; Multi-Raft in CockroachDB; Raft vs Paxos; a client whose write timed out (it may have committed, so use idempotency keys).
keyPoints: Raft turns a group of 3 or 5 machines into one replicated log; every replica applies the same commands in the same order
An entry is committed once the leader has it on a majority and it is from the leader's current term; older entries commit indirectly
The election restriction (vote only for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date) is what makes committed entries survive leader changes
Reads are only linearizable if the leader proves it is still leader (ReadIndex) or holds a time-based lease
Raft and Multi-Paxos solve the same problem; Raft's strong leader and no-holes log make it easier to implement and reason about
interview: Walk through Raft log replication: when is an entry committed, and why can a new leader not commit old-term entries by counting replicas?
Why does a Raft cluster need an odd number of nodes, and what happens during a network partition?
Raft vs Paxos: what is the actual difference, and why did etcd and CockroachDB pick Raft?
How do you serve linearizable reads in a Raft-based system without writing every read to the log?

check.q: A 5-node Raft cluster loses 2 nodes. What happens to writes?
options: Writes stop until all 5 nodes are back
Writes continue, because 3 of 5 is still a majority
Writes continue but are no longer durable
The cluster automatically shrinks to 3 nodes and then needs all 3
check.why: A majority of the configured membership (3 of 5) can still elect a leader and commit entries. Losing a third node would stop writes.

check.q: Why does a Raft follower refuse to vote for a candidate whose last log entry has a lower term than its own?
options: Because the candidate might be missing committed entries, and electing it could erase them
To keep elections fast
Because terms must always increase by exactly one
To prevent two leaders from sending heartbeats
check.why: Committed entries live on a majority. Any winning candidate needs votes from a majority, so at least one voter has every committed entry and blocks a candidate with a staler log.

check.q: A Raft leader serves reads from local state without any check. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, the leader always has the latest data
Reads become slower than writes
A deposed leader in a minority partition can return stale data after a new leader has committed newer writes
Followers will reject the next AppendEntries
check.why: A partitioned old leader may not know it was replaced. ReadIndex (confirm leadership with a heartbeat round) or a clock-bounded lease is needed for linearizable reads.

lessons.title: Replication models: single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless
lessons.summary: The three ways to replicate data, what each costs in latency and correctness, the anomalies replication lag causes, how quorums really behave, and where CRDTs fit.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Replication means keeping copies of the same data on several machines: to survive failures, to put data near users, and to spread read load. Copying data that never changes is trivial. All of the difficulty is in **changes**: who is allowed to accept a write, how the write reaches the other copies, and what readers see while it is in flight.

Kleppmann's *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* (chapter 5) sorts every replicated database into three models, and that framing is the one interviewers expect:

```text
single-leader   writes -> [L] -> F1, F2         one place decides the order
multi-leader    writes -> [L1] <-> [L2] <-> [L3] each region accepts writes
leaderless      writes -> any W of N replicas     client or coordinator fans out
```

The question behind all three is the same: **where can a write be accepted, and what happens when two writes to the same data happen concurrently?**

## Single-leader replication
One replica is the leader (primary). All writes go to it; it writes them to its log and streams the log to followers (replicas, standbys), which apply it in the same order. Reads can go to the leader (fresh) or followers (cheaper, possibly stale). PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL replication, MongoDB replica sets, SQL Server availability groups and most managed databases work this way. Raft groups are single-leader too, with a majority commit rule on top.

### Sync, async, semi-sync
- **Synchronous**: the leader waits for a follower to confirm before acknowledging the client. No acknowledged write is lost if the leader dies, but a slow or dead follower stalls writes.
- **Asynchronous**: the leader acknowledges immediately. Fast and tolerant of slow followers, but writes in the replication pipe are lost on failover.
- **Semi-synchronous / quorum**: wait for one (or a majority) of followers. PostgreSQL expresses this with `synchronous_standby_names` (for example `ANY 1 (s1, s2)`) and `synchronous_commit`; MongoDB with `writeConcern: { w: "majority" }`.

### What the log contains
- **Statement-based**: ship the SQL. Breaks on non-deterministic functions like `NOW()` or `RANDOM()`.
- **Physical / WAL shipping**: ship the storage engine's byte-level changes. Exact, but ties replicas to the same engine version.
- **Logical (row-based)**: ship "row with key K now has these values". Version-independent and readable by other systems, which is why change data capture (Debezium, Postgres logical decoding) builds on it.

### Failover is where it hurts
Detecting a dead leader needs a timeout, and timeouts are guesses. Common failures:
- **Lost writes**: with async replication the new leader lacks the old leader's tail. DDIA recounts a GitHub incident where a promoted, out-of-date MySQL follower reused auto-increment ids that were also stored in Redis, so some private data was shown to the wrong users.
- **Split brain**: the old leader is alive but partitioned, and both accept writes. You need fencing (the old leader is shut off or its writes rejected by a higher epoch or term) not just a new leader.
- **Flapping**: a timeout that is too short triggers failover during a load spike, which adds load and causes another failover.

This is why managed failover (Patroni with etcd, MongoDB's Raft-like elections, Aurora's storage-level quorum) uses consensus to pick the new leader rather than a script.

## Replication lag and the anomalies users see
With async followers, a follower may be milliseconds or minutes behind. Three anomalies follow, each with a specific fix.

```text
read-your-writes   I post a comment, reload, and it is gone (read hit a lagging follower)
monotonic reads    I see a comment, reload, and it disappears (second read hit a more-lagging follower)
consistent prefix  I see an answer before the question it replies to (partitions replicate at different speeds)
```

- **Read-your-writes**: read your own data from the leader (for example "a user's own profile always from the leader"), or for a short window after the user writes, or track the log position of their last write (Postgres LSN, MongoDB `operationTime`) and only read from a replica that has applied at least that position. MongoDB's causally consistent sessions do exactly this.
- **Monotonic reads**: pin each user to one replica (hash the user id), so they never go backwards in time.
- **Consistent prefix**: keep causally related writes in the same partition, or carry causal dependencies explicitly.

These are guarantees about one user's view. They are weaker than linearizability, which promises everyone sees one up-to-date copy, and much cheaper.

## Multi-leader replication
Several nodes accept writes, typically one leader per datacenter, and they replicate to each other asynchronously.

Where it makes sense:
- **Multi-region writes** with local latency: each region writes locally and syncs in the background.
- **Offline clients**: every phone or laptop with a local database is effectively a leader (CouchDB/PouchDB, mobile sync, local-first apps).
- **Collaborative editing**: every open document is a local replica.

The cost is **write conflicts**. Two regions update the same row concurrently and both succeed locally. You find out later, when there is no user left to ask. Resolution options:
- **Avoid conflicts**: route all writes for a given record to one "home" leader. Simple and common, but you lose the benefit when the home region is down.
- **Last write wins (LWW)**: keep the version with the highest timestamp and silently drop the other. Clock skew decides which write survives.
- **Merge**: union the values, keep siblings for the application to resolve, or use a CRDT.

Topology matters too. In a ring or star, a write must pass through intermediate leaders, and one failure breaks the chain; with all-to-all replication, writes can arrive out of causal order (an update before the insert it modifies), which needs version vectors to detect.

## Leaderless replication
Amazon's 2007 Dynamo paper popularised this model; Cassandra, ScyllaDB and Riak follow it. (Despite the name, Amazon DynamoDB the service uses a leader per partition with Paxos.) Any replica accepts writes. The client, or a coordinator node acting for it, sends each write to all `n` replicas of a key and waits for `w` acknowledgements; a read asks replicas and waits for `r` responses, picking the newest version.

```text
n = 3 replicas, w = 2, r = 2

write v2:  A ok  B ok  C (down)      -> success, w=2 reached
read:      A v2  C v1                -> client sees both, returns v2,
                                        and writes v2 back to C (read repair)
```

If `w + r > n`, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica, so a read normally sees the latest acknowledged write. Missing data is healed by **read repair** (fix stale replicas found during a read) and **anti-entropy** (a background process compares replicas, often with Merkle trees). Cassandra exposes this as consistency levels: `ONE`, `QUORUM`, `LOCAL_QUORUM`, `ALL` per query.

### Why quorums still return stale data
`w + r > n` is necessary, not sufficient. Kleppmann lists the edge cases, and Jepsen has demonstrated several in real systems:
- **Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff**: if the home replicas are unreachable, the write lands on other nodes and is handed back later. The overlap guarantee is gone until then.
- **Concurrent writes with LWW**: two writes race, and the one with the higher (possibly skewed) timestamp wins. An acknowledged write can vanish.
- **Write concurrent with a read**: the read may see the new value on one replica and not the other; which one wins is undefined.
- **Partial failure**: a write that reached fewer than `w` replicas is reported as failed but is not rolled back on the ones that took it. Later reads may return it.
- **Replica restore**: a node rebuilt from a stale replica can drop below the number of fresh copies.
- **Not linearizable**: reader 1 sees the new value, then reader 2 (later in real time) sees the old one, unless reads perform synchronous read repair before returning, and even then concurrent writes break it.

Quorums give you a tunable, usually-fresh store that stays available when nodes die. They do not give you compare-and-set or uniqueness. For that you need consensus (Cassandra's lightweight transactions use Paxos for exactly this).

## Detecting concurrency and merging: version vectors and CRDTs
Two writes are **concurrent** when neither knew about the other, not when they happened at the same wall-clock time. **Version vectors** (one counter per replica) detect this: if neither vector dominates the other, keep both versions as siblings.

Then something must merge them. **CRDTs** (conflict-free replicated data types, Shapiro et al. 2011) are data types whose merge is commutative, associative and idempotent, so replicas that have seen the same set of updates converge regardless of order or duplication.

```ts
// G-Counter: each replica only increments its own slot; merge takes the max per slot.
type GCounter = Record<string, number>;

export function increment(c: GCounter, replica: string, by = 1): GCounter {
  return { ...c, [replica]: (c[replica] ?? 0) + by };
}

export function merge(a: GCounter, b: GCounter): GCounter {
  const out: GCounter = { ...a };
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(b)) out[k] = Math.max(out[k] ?? 0, v);
  return out;
}

export const value = (c: GCounter) => Object.values(c).reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0);
```

Max per slot is idempotent (merging twice changes nothing) and order-independent, which is why it survives duplicate and reordered messages. Other common CRDTs: PN-counter (two G-counters for increments and decrements), OR-set (add-wins set that handles remove-then-re-add correctly), LWW-register, and sequence CRDTs for collaborative text (Yjs, Automerge). Riak shipped CRDT data types; Redis Enterprise's Active-Active databases use them for multi-region writes.

The limit: CRDTs guarantee convergence, not business invariants. A PN-counter balance converges, but two regions can each approve a withdrawal and drive it negative. Anything of the form "at most one", "never below zero" or "unique" needs coordination.

## Choosing: a worked example
**Global shopping cart, users in three regions.** Adding an item must never fail, and a merged cart is acceptable (an extra item can be removed at checkout). That is the original Dynamo use case: leaderless or multi-leader with a set-like merge. Use an OR-set rather than a plain union, or deleted items come back, which was a known quirk of Dynamo's original union merge.

**Checkout and payment.** Must not double-charge or oversell. Single leader (or a consensus-backed database) for the order and inventory rows, with an idempotency key on the payment call.

**User profile.** Single leader with async followers, plus read-your-writes for the profile owner.

One system can, and usually should, use more than one model.

## Trade-offs at a glance
| Model | Write latency | Writes during partition | Conflicts | Typical systems |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Single-leader | One region (plus sync replicas) | Only on the leader's side | None (one order) | Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB |
| Multi-leader | Local | Yes, every region | Yes, must resolve | CouchDB, multi-region active-active setups |
| Leaderless | Fastest w of n | Yes, with sloppy quorum | Yes, LWW or siblings | Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak |

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Reading from replicas by default** and then debugging "random" missing data. Measure lag (`pg_stat_replication.replay_lag` in Postgres, `rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo()` in MongoDB) and decide per query whether staleness is acceptable.
- **Assuming lag is small**. It is usually small; under a long-running transaction, a vacuum, a backup or a network blip it can be minutes.
- **Relying on LWW for anything users care about**. It loses writes silently and depends on clocks.
- **Treating `QUORUM` as strongly consistent**. Check for sloppy quorums and LWW before promising "no stale reads".
- **Automatic failover without fencing**, leading to split brain.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you can match a replication model to a product requirement and name the failure modes, not just define the terms.

**60-second answer outline:**
1. Single-leader: one write order, simple; risks are failover and replica lag. Default choice.
2. Multi-leader: local writes in each region or offline; you must resolve conflicts (avoid by home region, LWW, or merge with CRDTs).
3. Leaderless: quorum reads and writes, stays writable through node loss; `w + r > n` overlap, read repair and anti-entropy; still not linearizable.
4. Replication lag anomalies (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix) and their fixes.
5. Choose per data type: carts merge, money coordinates.

**Follow-ups to expect:** sync vs async trade-off for failover; how MongoDB or Postgres give read-your-writes; why `QUORUM` can still be stale; what a CRDT cannot do; how you would detect and handle split brain.
keyPoints: Single-leader gives one order of writes and simple reasoning; its risks are failover (lost async writes, split brain) and replica lag
Multi-leader and leaderless accept writes in many places, so concurrent writes conflict and you must choose how to merge them
Replication lag breaks read-your-writes, monotonic reads and consistent prefix; fix each one deliberately, not by hoping lag is small
w + r > n makes read and write quorums overlap but does not by itself give linearizability; sloppy quorums and LWW break it
CRDTs make merges automatic and convergent for specific data types (counters, sets, text), not for invariants like balances
interview: Compare single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication. Which would you pick for a global shopping cart?
What replication-lag anomalies can users see, and how do you guarantee read-your-writes?
In a leaderless store with N=3, W=2 and R=2, can a client still read stale data?

check.q: A user updates their profile, refreshes, and sees the old value. Reads go to async followers. Which guarantee is missing?
options: Monotonic reads
Consistent prefix reads
Read-your-writes
Linearizability of other users' writes
check.why: The user cannot see their own write because the follower has not caught up. Route their reads to the leader for a while, or wait until the follower has applied the write's log position.

check.q: With async replication, the leader fails and a follower is promoted. What is the main data risk?
options: Writes acknowledged by the old leader but not yet replicated are lost
The new leader will reject all reads
Indexes must be rebuilt from scratch
Clients must re-authenticate
check.why: Async means the leader acknowledged before followers had the write. Promoting a follower discards that tail; if the old leader comes back it must drop it too.

check.q: Which data is the best fit for a CRDT rather than a single leader?
options: A bank balance that must never go negative
A unique username registry
A like counter updated from several regions
An auction where only one highest bid may win
check.why: A counter merges naturally (sum of per-replica increments). Non-negative balances, uniqueness and single winners are invariants that need coordination.

lessons.title: Partitioning (sharding): keys, rebalancing, hot spots and indexes
lessons.summary: How to split data across machines: range vs hash partitioning, consistent hashing, rebalancing strategies, hot partitions, secondary indexes across shards and request routing.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Replication copies the same data to several machines. **Partitioning** (sharding) splits the data so each machine holds a different subset. You partition when one machine can no longer hold the data or absorb the write rate. In practice you do both: each partition is replicated, so a node holds replicas of several partitions.

The goal is to spread data **and load** evenly. If one partition gets a disproportionate share, it is **hot**, and your 10-node cluster behaves like a 1-node cluster with extra bills. Every design decision below is about avoiding that while keeping common queries on one partition.

Two terms that vary by product: MongoDB calls them chunks on shards, Cassandra calls them token ranges, CockroachDB and HBase call them ranges or regions, Elasticsearch calls them shards, DynamoDB calls them partitions. Same idea.

## Step 1: pick the partition key
The partition key is the attribute that decides which partition owns a row. The test is your access patterns:

- Queries that include the key go to one partition. Good.
- Queries that do not include it must ask every partition (**scatter-gather**). Acceptable for rare analytics, deadly for a hot path.
- The key must have enough distinct values, spread evenly, to fill many partitions, and its **write** distribution must be even too.

A good key is usually the thing your hottest queries are "about": `tenant_id` in B2B SaaS, `user_id` for a personal feed, `channel_id` for messages, `order_id` for order lookups.

## Range partitioning
Assign contiguous key ranges to partitions, like volumes of an encyclopedia: `[a, f)`, `[f, m)`, and so on. Boundaries can be chosen manually or, better, by the database splitting ranges as they grow.

```text
range partitioning on (user_id, ts)
  [0000.. , 3000..)  -> node A
  [3000.. , 7000..)  -> node B
  [7000.. , ffff..)  -> node C
  scan user 4123 for last week -> one range, contiguous on disk
```

Strengths: range scans and ordered iteration are cheap, and related keys sit together. Bigtable, HBase, CockroachDB, Spanner, TiKV and MongoDB ranged sharding use it.

Weakness: **monotonic keys**. If the key is a timestamp or an auto-increment id, every insert goes to the last range, so one node takes all writes while others idle. Fixes: lead the key with something high-cardinality (`(sensor_id, ts)` instead of `ts`), hash-prefix it, or use random ids (UUIDv4) where ordering is not needed. CockroachDB's docs recommend exactly this, and it is why its hash-sharded indexes exist.

## Hash partitioning
Apply a hash function to the key and partition by hash value. A decent hash (Murmur3 in Cassandra, MD5 in MongoDB hashed sharding) spreads even skewed or sequential keys uniformly.

The cost: adjacent keys are scattered, so range queries on the hashed key must hit every partition.

The best of both is a **compound key**: hash the first part to pick the partition, keep the rest sorted within it. Cassandra's primary key `((channel_id, bucket), message_id)` hashes `(channel_id, bucket)` and stores messages sorted by `message_id` inside; DynamoDB's partition key plus sort key is the same idea. You get even distribution across entities and efficient range scans within one.

## Rebalancing: never hash mod N
Data grows and nodes come and go, so partitions must move. The naive placement `node = hash(key) % N` is a trap: going from N to N+1 nodes changes the result for about N/(N+1) of keys. From 10 to 11 nodes, roughly 91% of data moves.

Three strategies that move only what is necessary:

**1. Many fixed partitions.** Create far more partitions than nodes (say 1,024 for 10 nodes) and assign whole partitions to nodes. A new node steals a few partitions from each existing one; keys never change partition. Elasticsearch (shard count fixed at index creation), Couchbase (1,024 vBuckets) and Riak use this. Downside: you must guess the count up front; too few and partitions get huge, too many and overhead grows.

**2. Dynamic splitting.** Split a range when it exceeds a size (CockroachDB's default range max is 512 MiB; MongoDB splits chunks) and merge small ones. Partition count adapts to data. Downside: a new empty table starts as one range on one node until it splits; some systems let you pre-split.

**3. Consistent hashing.** Map both nodes and keys onto a ring of hash values; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding a node takes over only the arc before it, about 1/N of keys. With one point per node the arcs are uneven, so each node gets many **virtual nodes** (tokens). Cassandra uses this (`num_tokens`, default 16 in 4.0 with a smarter allocation algorithm). Variants: **rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing**, and Google's **jump consistent hash** (Lamping and Veach), which needs no ring and almost no memory but only supports numbered buckets that grow or shrink at the end.

```text
consistent hash ring (virtual nodes)
      A1      B1
  C2              A2
  B2              C1
      A3      B3
key k hashes between A2 and C1 -> owned by C1 (node C)
add node D: it takes a few arcs from A, B and C; other keys do not move
```

Whatever the strategy, **automatic vs manual** rebalancing matters. Fully automatic moves can combine badly with failure detection: a slow node is declared dead, its data is copied elsewhere, the copying overloads the cluster, more nodes look dead. Many operators keep a human in the loop for large moves, and every system throttles rebalancing bandwidth.

## Hot spots: when one key is the problem
Even partitioning cannot help when a **single key** is hot: a celebrity's timeline, a viral product, a global counter. The database cannot split one key across nodes; the application must.

- **Key salting / write sharding**: write to `product#123#7`, where the suffix is random in 0..N-1. Writes spread over N partitions; reads must query all N and combine. DynamoDB's docs describe this as write sharding. Only do it for keys you know are hot, because it multiplies read cost.
- **Split the entity**: count likes in N shard counters and sum them periodically.
- **Cache reads**: a hot read key belongs in a cache or CDN, often with request coalescing so a cache miss produces one database read, not thousands.
- **Bucket by time**: Discord's 2017 post explains how messages are partitioned by `(channel_id, bucket)` where the bucket is a fixed time window, so one busy channel does not become an unbounded partition. Their 2023 follow-up describes moving to ScyllaDB and adding data services that coalesce concurrent requests for the same channel, because hot partitions were still their main source of latency.
- **Managed help**: DynamoDB's adaptive capacity shifts throughput to hot partitions and can split them, but a single partition still has per-partition limits (on the order of 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second), so one key cannot exceed that.

Detect hot spots with per-partition metrics: request rate and latency per shard, top keys (Redis `--hotkeys`, DynamoDB Contributor Insights, CockroachDB's hot ranges page).

## Secondary indexes across partitions
A secondary index lets you find rows by something other than the partition key, such as orders by `product_id`. Two designs:

```text
LOCAL (document-partitioned)                GLOBAL (term-partitioned)
partition 1: orders 1..  + index on its rows   index itself partitioned by product_id
partition 2: orders ..   + index on its rows   product 'p9' entries all on index partition 3
write: one partition                          write: row partition + index partition(s)
read by product: ask every partition          read by product: one index partition
```

- **Local indexes** (MongoDB, Cassandra secondary indexes, Elasticsearch): each partition indexes its own rows. Writes stay local and simple; reads by the indexed field are scatter-gather, and tail latency is the slowest partition. With 100 partitions, a 1% chance of a slow partition makes most queries slow.
- **Global indexes** (DynamoDB GSIs, CockroachDB and Spanner secondary indexes): the index is partitioned by the indexed value. Reads go to one index partition; writes must update the row and one or more index partitions. DynamoDB keeps GSIs **eventually consistent** to avoid a distributed transaction on every write; CockroachDB and Spanner update them **transactionally**, paying a cross-range commit.

A third, very common, option: keep the primary store partitioned by its natural key and maintain a **separate search or analytics store** (Elasticsearch, a warehouse) fed by change data capture for the other access patterns.

## Request routing
Something must know which node owns which partition:
- A **routing tier** that knows the map (MongoDB's `mongos` reading config servers, Vitess's VTGate).
- **Any node** accepts the request and forwards it (Cassandra coordinators, with ring state spread by gossip).
- **Partition-aware clients** that cache the map and route directly (Cassandra and ScyllaDB drivers, Redis Cluster clients following `MOVED` redirects).

Metadata itself usually lives in a consensus system (ZooKeeper, etcd, or the database's own Raft group) because every node must agree on it.

## Worked example: 10 TB of user events
Requirements: append-heavy (say 50k events per second), queries are "events for user U in a time window" and occasionally "all events of type T yesterday".

1. **Key**: `(user_id, event_time, event_id)`. Partition by `user_id` (hashed), sort by time within a user. User queries hit one partition and read a contiguous slice.
2. **Writes spread** across users by the hash. No single "now" hot spot because time is not the leading key.
3. **Heavy users**: if a few bots or enterprise tenants dominate, add a bucket: `(user_id, month)` as the partition key so a user's history is split into bounded partitions.
4. **Type-T queries**: do not scan the OLTP store. Stream events to a columnar store (BigQuery, ClickHouse, Snowflake) partitioned by date.
5. **Retention**: time buckets make dropping old data a cheap partition drop instead of a giant delete.

```sql
-- Cassandra/ScyllaDB style table for the hot path
CREATE TABLE events_by_user (
  user_id    uuid,
  month      text,          -- '2026-10', bounds partition size
  event_time timestamp,
  event_id   timeuuid,
  type       text,
  payload    blob,
  PRIMARY KEY ((user_id, month), event_time, event_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (event_time DESC, event_id DESC);
```

## Trade-offs and when not to shard
Sharding is a one-way door that complicates joins, transactions, unique constraints, backups and schema changes. Before sharding a relational database, exhaust the cheaper options: better indexes, read replicas, caching, archiving cold data, a bigger machine (single Postgres instances handle many terabytes), or a distributed SQL database that shards for you. Shard when the write rate or working set truly exceeds one machine, or for tenant isolation.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Choosing the key from the data model rather than the queries.**
- **Monotonic leading keys** in range-partitioned stores.
- **Low-cardinality keys** (country, status): a few huge partitions you can never split.
- **Unbounded partitions**: one tenant or channel grows forever; add a time or hash bucket.
- **Cross-shard queries on the hot path**, discovered when p99 latency explodes as the shard count grows.
- **Debugging**: look at per-partition request rate, size and latency; skew shows up as one shard's p99 far above the rest.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you design the key from access patterns, know why range vs hash matters, can handle a hot key, and understand the cost of secondary indexes.

**60-second answer outline:**
1. List the access patterns; pick a high-cardinality key that hot queries include.
2. Range for scans, hash for even spread, compound key for both.
3. Rebalance with fixed partitions, splitting or consistent hashing, never mod N.
4. Hot keys need salting, splitting, caching or coalescing.
5. Local indexes scatter reads, global indexes cost cross-partition writes; or push secondary access patterns to a search or analytics store via CDC.

**Follow-ups to expect:** how you would reshard live (double writes or a fixed-partition move, then cut over); how unique constraints work across shards; how you keep a tenant's data together; what consistent hashing's virtual nodes fix.
keyPoints: The partition key decides everything: which queries hit one shard, which fan out, and where hot spots appear
Range partitioning keeps scans cheap but turns monotonic keys (timestamps, sequences) into a single hot shard; hashing spreads load but loses ranges
Never use hash mod N for placement: adding a node moves almost every key. Use many fixed partitions, dynamic splitting or consistent hashing
Hot keys need application help: salting, splitting, caching or request coalescing; the database cannot split one key
Local secondary indexes make writes cheap and reads scatter-gather; global indexes make reads targeted and writes cross-partition
interview: How would you partition a 10 TB table of user events? Walk through choosing the key.
How do you handle a hot partition, for example a celebrity account or a viral product?
How do secondary indexes work in a partitioned database, and what is the difference between local and global indexes?

check.q: A table is range-partitioned on created_at. Writes are slow and one node is at 100% CPU. Why?
options: Range partitioning cannot use indexes
All new writes have the latest timestamp, so they all land in the last range on one node
The table needs more replicas
Timestamps are too large to hash
check.why: Monotonic keys concentrate every insert at the end of the key space. Prefix the key with something high-cardinality (user id, a hash bucket) or hash it.

check.q: You place keys with hash(key) mod N and grow from 10 to 11 nodes. Roughly what fraction of keys move?
options: About 1/11
About 1/2
About 10/11
None, existing keys stay put
check.why: A key stays only if hash mod 10 equals hash mod 11, which holds for about 1 in 11 keys. Consistent hashing or fixed partitions move only about 1/11.

check.q: Orders are partitioned by customer_id. A query filters by product_id using a local (per-partition) secondary index. What happens?
options: It reads exactly one partition
It fails, local indexes only support the partition key
It is sent to every partition and the results are merged (scatter-gather)
It reads the global index on the coordinator
check.why: Each partition indexes only its own rows, so any partition might hold matching orders. Tail latency becomes the slowest partition.

lessons.title: Distributed transactions: 2PC, sagas, Spanner, Percolator and Calvin
lessons.summary: How to make a change atomic across machines or services: two-phase commit and why it blocks, sagas and compensation, Spanner's TrueTime, Percolator's lock columns and Calvin's deterministic ordering.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A transaction is **atomic** if either all its writes happen or none do. On one machine the database gets this from a write-ahead log: the commit record is a single write that is either on disk or not. Once the writes live on **different machines** (different shards of one database, or different services with their own databases), there is no single commit record, and each machine can crash independently. A distributed transaction protocol must make every participant reach the **same decision** despite crashes and message loss.

There are two families:
- **Atomic commit inside one system**: 2PC, usually hardened with consensus (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB), or avoided by deterministic ordering (Calvin).
- **Business-level consistency across services**: sagas, the outbox pattern and idempotency, accepting that intermediate states are visible.

Knowing which family a question is about is half the interview.

## Two-phase commit (2PC)
A **coordinator** (often the node or service the client talked to) drives **participants** (the shards or resource managers holding the data).

```text
            coordinator                 participant A       participant B
phase 1     PREPARE  ------------------>  write data+locks durably
                                         vote YES <--------
            PREPARE  ----------------------------------->   vote YES
            log decision COMMIT (the commit point)
phase 2     COMMIT   ------------------>  apply, release locks, ack
            COMMIT   ----------------------------------->   apply, ack
```

1. **Prepare**: each participant does all the work, writes it durably, takes the locks, and promises it can commit no matter what (no constraint violation, no crash will lose it). Then it votes YES. Any NO aborts everything.
2. **Decide**: if all vote YES, the coordinator writes COMMIT to its own durable log. **That write is the commit point.**
3. **Commit**: the coordinator tells everyone, retrying forever until each acknowledges.

Two promises make it work: a participant that voted YES can never later abort on its own, and the coordinator's decision is irrevocable once logged.

### The blocking problem
If the coordinator crashes after participants voted YES but before they learn the decision, they are **in doubt**. They cannot abort (the coordinator might have logged COMMIT and told someone else) and cannot commit (it might have decided ABORT). They must hold their locks until the coordinator recovers. Meanwhile every other transaction touching those rows waits. In XA deployments, in-doubt transactions sometimes need a human to resolve them.

Other costs: at least two round trips plus several fsyncs per transaction, latency bound by the slowest participant, and locks held across network calls. Three-phase commit tries to remove blocking but assumes bounded network delays, so it is rarely used in practice.

### How modern databases fix it
The coordinator's state is the problem, so **replicate it**. In Spanner, each participant is a Paxos group and the coordinator is the leader of one of them; the prepare and commit records are written through consensus, so a single machine's crash does not lose the decision. CockroachDB stores a **transaction record** in the range of the transaction's first key, replicated by Raft; any node finding an intent can look up the record to learn the transaction's status. Its **parallel commits** optimisation writes the intents and a STAGING record in parallel, so a commit costs roughly one round of consensus instead of two. The protocol is still 2PC; the coordinator just cannot disappear.

## Sagas: transactions across services
Across microservices with separate databases (or with third parties like a payment provider), 2PC is usually not an option: the services do not support XA, and holding locks across a slow external call is unacceptable. The **saga** (Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987) replaces one long transaction with a sequence of **local transactions**, each with a **compensating transaction** that semantically undoes it.

```text
transfer 100 from account A (Accounts svc) to account B (Ledger svc)

T1  reserve 100 on A          C1  release reservation on A
T2  credit 100 to B (pending) C2  reverse the pending credit
T3  finalise: debit A, settle B   (pivot: after this, only forward recovery)

failure at T3 -> run C2, then C1
```

Key design points:
- **Compensations are new business actions**, not rollbacks. A sent email cannot be unsent; you send a correction. A charge is refunded, not erased.
- **Every step and compensation must be idempotent** and retriable, because messages are delivered at least once.
- **Pivot step**: the point after which the saga can only go forward (retry until success). Order steps so risky, reversible ones come before the pivot.
- **No isolation**: other transactions can see intermediate states (A's money reserved but B not credited). Countermeasures: **semantic locks** (a `PENDING` status others respect), commutative updates, re-reading values before acting, and putting the riskiest step last.
- **Orchestration vs choreography**: a central orchestrator (a workflow engine such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions, or your own state machine table) drives steps and compensations explicitly; in choreography each service reacts to the previous service's events. Orchestration is easier to reason about and monitor once there are more than two or three steps.
- **Reliable step boundaries**: each service must update its database and publish its event atomically, which is the **transactional outbox** pattern (write the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction, relay it afterwards).

```ts
// Orchestrator step with idempotency: safe to run twice.
async function reserveFunds(sagaId: string, accountId: string, amount: number) {
  await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const done = await tx.query(
      "SELECT 1 FROM saga_steps WHERE saga_id = $1 AND step = 'reserve'", [sagaId]);
    if (done.rowCount) return; // already applied
    const r = await tx.query(
      "UPDATE accounts SET available = available - $2 WHERE id = $1 AND available >= $2",
      [accountId, amount]);
    if (r.rowCount === 0) throw new InsufficientFunds(accountId);
    await tx.query(
      "INSERT INTO saga_steps (saga_id, step) VALUES ($1, 'reserve')", [sagaId]);
    await tx.query(
      "INSERT INTO outbox (topic, payload) VALUES ('funds.reserved', $1)",
      [JSON.stringify({ sagaId, accountId, amount })]);
  });
}
```

## Spanner and TrueTime
Spanner (Corbett et al., OSDI 2012) is a globally distributed SQL database that offers **external consistency**: if transaction T1 commits before T2 starts (in real time), T1's commit timestamp is smaller than T2's. That is strict serializability, the strongest standard isolation guarantee. Data is split into ranges (splits), each replicated with Paxos; multi-split transactions use 2PC across Paxos groups as described above, with strict two-phase locking for read-write transactions.

The hard part is timestamps. Clocks on different machines disagree. Spanner's **TrueTime** API does not pretend otherwise: `TT.now()` returns an **interval** `[earliest, latest]` guaranteed to contain true time. Google keeps the interval small with GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every datacenter; the paper reports uncertainty (epsilon) typically under about 7 ms.

**Commit wait**: the leader picks commit timestamp `s >= TT.now().latest`, then **waits until `TT.now().earliest > s`** before making the commit visible and releasing locks. After the wait, `s` is in the past on every correct clock, so any transaction that starts later will get a larger timestamp. The cost is a wait of about twice epsilon per read-write transaction, overlapped with the Paxos replication.

The payoff: **lock-free snapshot reads**. A read-only transaction picks a timestamp and reads from any sufficiently up-to-date replica without locks, with a consistent view across the whole database.

Systems without atomic clocks use **hybrid logical clocks** instead. CockroachDB assumes a maximum clock offset (500 ms by default) and gives each transaction an **uncertainty interval**: if it reads a value with a timestamp inside that window, it cannot tell whether the write happened before it, so it moves its own timestamp forward and may restart. It offers serializability and avoids stale reads for single keys, but not Spanner's full external consistency across unrelated keys, and nodes whose clocks drift too far shut themselves down.

## Percolator: transactions on a key-value store
Google built Percolator (Peng and Dabek, OSDI 2010) to update the web search index incrementally on top of **Bigtable**, which only had single-row atomicity. It adds multi-row **snapshot isolation** using three ingredients:
- A **timestamp oracle**: a central service handing out strictly increasing timestamps (in batches, for throughput).
- Extra **columns** per cell: `data` (versioned values), `lock` (pending writes) and `write` (commit records pointing at a data version).
- A **primary lock**: one of the transaction's cells is chosen as primary; every other lock points to it.

```text
start_ts = oracle()
reads: at start_ts; if a lock older than start_ts is found, wait or clean it up
PREWRITE (phase 1), for each cell, primary first:
   abort if a write record newer than start_ts exists (write-write conflict)
   abort if any lock exists
   write data@start_ts and lock@start_ts -> primary
commit_ts = oracle()
COMMIT (phase 2):
   on the primary row (single-row atomic): check our lock still exists,
   write write@commit_ts -> start_ts, erase lock     <- THE COMMIT POINT
   then secondaries: write record + erase lock (can be lazy/asynchronous)
```

The trick is that **the commit point is a single-row atomic operation on the primary**. There is no separate coordinator to lose. If a client crashes mid-commit, the next reader that hits a stale secondary lock checks the primary: if the primary has a write record, roll the secondary forward; if the primary lock is still there and old, roll it back. Recovery is lazy and distributed.

The costs: every transaction needs two oracle round trips, writes take several Bigtable operations, and crashed clients leave locks that slow readers until cleaned up. Percolator suits throughput-oriented workloads. **TiDB/TiKV** adopted the Percolator model (with a Placement Driver as the timestamp oracle), with later optimisations such as async commit and one-phase commit for single-region transactions.

## Calvin: agree on the order first
Calvin (Thomson et al., SIGMOD 2012) asks why 2PC is needed at all. The answer is non-determinism: a participant might abort on its own (deadlock, crash, constraint), so the others must ask. Calvin removes that:

1. A **sequencing layer** collects transaction requests into short batches (epochs of about 10 ms in the paper) and replicates the batch order with consensus. Now every replica agrees on a **global order of inputs** before any execution.
2. A **scheduler** on each partition acquires locks in that exact order and executes deterministically. Every replica executing the same input order reaches the same result, so there is no need to vote on the outcome; a crashed replica recovers by replaying the input log.

Trade-offs: transactions must declare their read and write sets up front. Transactions whose keys depend on reads (look up an index, then update the row it points to) need a reconnaissance read first and a retry if the set changed. Interactive transactions (BEGIN, chat with the app, COMMIT) do not fit. FaunaDB was built on Calvin-style ideas; Daniel Abadi's writing on deterministic databases is the best follow-up.

## Choosing
Inside one distributed database, use its built-in transactions. Across your own services or a third party, use a saga with an outbox, idempotent steps and periodic reconciliation. Reserve XA for resource managers that all support it in one datacenter. Often the best option is to **redraw the boundary** so data that must change atomically lives in one service and one database.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Saying "use 2PC" across microservices** without addressing blocking, XA support and lock duration.
- **Sagas without idempotency**: a retried message double-credits an account.
- **Compensations that can fail permanently** with no alert or manual path. Every saga needs a "stuck" state and a dashboard.
- **Ignoring the visibility of intermediate states** (the user sees money gone from A but not yet in B). Design the UI and status fields for it.
- **Assuming wall clocks order events** across machines, or retrying serialization failures without backoff.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** that you know 2PC's blocking failure mode, how real databases avoid it, when to use sagas instead, and that you can explain TrueTime without hand-waving.

**60-second answer outline:**
1. 2PC: prepare (durable, locked, promise), coordinator logs the decision, then commit. If the coordinator dies after YES votes, participants block holding locks.
2. Distributed databases replicate the coordinator with Paxos or Raft, so 2PC no longer depends on one machine.
3. Across services: saga of local transactions plus compensations, outbox for reliable events, idempotency everywhere, semantic locks for the missing isolation.
4. Spanner: TrueTime intervals plus commit wait give external consistency and lock-free snapshot reads.
5. Percolator: oracle timestamps and a primary lock make the commit point a single-row write. Calvin: agree on input order, execute deterministically, no 2PC.

**Follow-ups to expect:** what if a compensation fails; how CockroachDB gets by without atomic clocks; why Percolator needs a timestamp oracle; what kinds of transactions Calvin cannot run; how you would test a saga (fault injection at every step).
keyPoints: 2PC gives atomicity across participants, but a coordinator crash after prepare leaves participants holding locks until it recovers
Modern databases make 2PC safe by replicating the coordinator's decision with consensus (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB)
Across services you usually cannot use 2PC; sagas chain local transactions with compensations and give up isolation
Spanner's commit wait uses TrueTime's bounded clock uncertainty so timestamp order matches real-time order
Percolator builds snapshot-isolation transactions on a key-value store with a timestamp oracle and a primary lock; Calvin avoids 2PC by agreeing on order first
interview: Walk through two-phase commit. What happens if the coordinator crashes after participants have voted yes?
How does Google Spanner use TrueTime to provide external consistency?
Design a money transfer between two services that do not share a database.
What is Percolator, and how does it build transactions on top of a key-value store?

check.q: In 2PC, a participant has voted yes and then loses contact with the coordinator. What may it do?
options: Abort after a timeout to release its locks
Commit after a timeout, since it voted yes
Neither: it must wait (or ask other participants) because the coordinator may have decided either way
Become the coordinator and decide
check.why: After voting yes it has given up the right to abort unilaterally, and it does not know the decision. That is the blocking problem of 2PC.

check.q: What does Spanner's commit wait achieve?
options: It batches commits to improve throughput
It waits until the chosen commit timestamp is guaranteed to be in the past on every clock, so later transactions get larger timestamps
It waits for all replicas worldwide to apply the write
It waits for the client to confirm the commit
check.why: TrueTime returns an interval. Waiting out the uncertainty means any transaction that starts after this one commits will pick a higher timestamp, giving external consistency.

check.q: A saga's third step fails after steps one and two committed. What is the correct response?
options: Roll back steps one and two with a database ROLLBACK
Run compensating actions for steps two and one, in reverse order
Ignore the failure because each step committed locally
